as_told.title: Plato's account of Athens fighting Atlantis 9,000 years before

tellings.quote: Let me begin by observing first of all, that nine thousand was the sum of years which had elapsed since the war which was said to have taken place between those who dwelt outside the pillars of Heracles and all who dwelt within them; this war I am going to describe.
Then listen, Socrates, to a tale which, though strange, is certainly true, having been attested by Solon, who was the wisest of the seven sages.
And what is this ancient famous action of the Athenians, which Critias declared, on the authority of Solon, to be not a mere legend, but an actual fact?

Now the day was that day of the Apaturia which is called the Registration of Youth, at which, according to custom, our parents gave prizes for recitations, and the poems of several poets were recited by us boys, and many of us sang the poems of Solon, which at that time had not gone out of fashion.
For these histories tell of a mighty power which unprovoked made an expedition against the whole of Europe and Asia, and to which your city put an end.

plain: In two of Plato's dialogues, the Timaeus and the Critias, a speaker named Critias tells of a great war, nine thousand years earlier, between ancient Athens and the island power of Atlantis. The guests disagree about what kind of story it is. A guest named James Madden calls it a myth, "another good lie" told to Socrates. The researcher Matt LaCroix treats it as real early history, saying Plato and Plutarch describe "proto Athenians" who fought Atlantis. Michels recalls Plato putting the war 9,000 years back and telling it at a festival. If it were history, it would mean an advanced civilisation existed long before the ones we know. In Benjamin Jowett's translation, Critias says that "nine thousand was the sum of years" since the war, and the Timaeus speaks of "a mighty power which unprovoked made an expedition against the whole of Europe and Asia, and to which your city put an end." The text has Critias call it "a tale which, though strange, is certainly true, having been attested by Solon", whom it calls the wisest of the seven sages, and Socrates repeats that it is "not a mere legend, but an actual fact." Those are claims made by characters inside the dialogue. Whether Plato himself meant it as history or as a teaching story, the text leaves open. The festival is the Apaturia, where, Critias says, boys recited poems and he first heard the tale as a child.

discussion.text: Where the tellers call the Atlantis story a myth or a lie, in Jowett's translation of the Timaeus Critias calls it "a tale which, though strange, is certainly true" and Socrates repeats that it is "not a mere legend, but an actual fact". The festival in the text is the Apaturia, at which the elder Critias, nearly ninety, told the tale when the younger Critias was about ten; the younger retells it on the day of the goddess's festival.
